topic: Touch football and futsal: hamstrings and ankles

slides.headline: Touch or futsal after work this term?
slides.sub: Quick feet, sudden sprints, hard turns. Here's how to keep playing.

slides.title: Why these two cop it
slides.body: Both sports are short bursts: flat-out sprints, sharp stops and quick changes of direction. Hamstrings take the load at top speed and ankles take it on every cut and landing.

slides.title: Warm up like it's a game
slides.body: Ten minutes is plenty. Easy jog, leg swings, a few skips, then build to three or four short sprints with turns. Cold hamstrings and a first-minute sprint don't mix well.

slides.title: Train the hamstring long and strong
slides.body: Hamstrings usually strain while lengthening at speed. Exercises like Nordic curls and single-leg bridges, twice a week, help them tolerate that load. Start with low numbers and build gradually.

slides.title: Give your ankles some balance work
slides.body: Stand on one leg while brushing your teeth, then try it eyes closed or on a pillow. Add small hops side to side. Simple, but it trains the reactions a court needs.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A sudden grab at the back of the thigh, bruising, a rolled ankle you can't walk on, or one that keeps giving way are worth an assessment rather than playing on.

slides.headline: Want to play the whole season?
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD physios look at your sprinting, landing and strength, then build a plan around your games. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Touch football or futsal after work? Your hamstrings and ankles are doing most of the work. ⚽

Both games are built on short sprints, sharp turns and quick stops. That's exactly where hamstrings and ankles tend to complain, especially early in a new season.

A proper ten-minute warm-up, a couple of hamstring strength sessions a week and some simple balance work for your ankles can go a long way. A sudden grab in the back of the thigh or an ankle that keeps giving way is worth getting assessed.
